title: Stewart-Smith Haidinger, Inc. v. Avi-Truck, Inc.
lead: A corporation formed to own an unusual cargo aircraft recovered hull insurance even though it was unnamed and did not exist when negotiations began.

actors.name: Trans-Northern Aleutian
actors.role: Aircraft operator that arranged insurance and ultimately leased the plane.

actors.name: Avi-Truck
actors.role: Corporation formed by two mechanics and their wives to buy the aircraft.

actors.name: Jack Good and John Chapman
actors.role: Insurance broker and Stewart-Smith representative involved in arranging coverage.

proceedings: A bank’s loan suit prompted Avi-Truck’s third-party insurance claim. Partial summary judgment and a trial produced a $60,000 hull judgment as to fewer than all claims and parties; the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed.
limits: Assignment theories were not before the Supreme Court. Federal pilot-qualification applicability and the effect of a pre-loss policy containing the airworthiness exclusion were expressly reserved. Other claims in the multiparty litigation were not all resolved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An operator arranges coverage before ownership is settled
paragraphs: Trans-Northern Aleutian, called TNA, operated smaller aircraft and became interested in a surplus military Chase YC-122 for moving large equipment. Two employees ferried the unusually large, old twin-engine aircraft to Anchorage in December 1976. TNA explored several purchase arrangements before deciding it preferred to lease.

TNA’s president, Lloyd Sudder, sought insurance through broker Jack Good, who contacted John Chapman of Stewart-Smith. Good knew the plane’s make, model, unusual dimensions and age, and cargo-only purpose. The parties later disputed whether Sudder also disclosed its public-use status and the proposed lease. Nobody discussed an airworthiness certificate; Good assumed one existed. In practice the plane could not obtain a certificate for private cargo carriage for hire, although it could lawfully carry government cargo as a public-use aircraft.

Good issued a December 13 binder covering the ferry flight and subsequent ground risk. It contemplated freight carriage for hire, specified pilot qualifications, and referred to a forthcoming new policy.

sections.title: Avi-Truck buys the aircraft, which crashes soon after flight coverage begins
paragraphs: TNA mechanics Robert Murnan and Bob Coward and their wives formed Avi-Truck to purchase the plane. Incorporated December 20, Avi-Truck bought it December 29 and leased it to TNA January 14, 1977. The lease required $60,000 hull insurance, $1 million liability insurance, declaration copies for the lessor, and advance cancellation notice.

Flight coverage was added January 24. On January 31, during its second flight after takeoff from Anchorage, the aircraft crashed while carrying Bureau of Indian Affairs school supplies. Although the binder anticipated a new policy, insurers eventually added the plane to TNA’s existing fleet policy by endorsement issued February 8, after the loss. They denied coverage under exclusions in that later document.

sections.title: The purchase lender’s suit leads to an insurance judgment
paragraphs: Alaska Statebank sued Avi-Truck on the purchase loan. Avi-Truck brought a third-party claim against the broker and insurers for the insurance proceeds. On June 5, 1980 Judge Singleton granted partial summary judgment recognizing Avi-Truck’s right to sue and rejecting the airworthiness exclusion. After a five-day trial beginning July 20, 1981, Judge Souter found coverage despite alleged deficiencies in the pilots’ qualifications. The resulting $60,000 hull judgment was final as to fewer than all parties and claims.

The insurers appealed beneficiary status, coverage under both exclusions, and admission of testimony about Federal Aviation Administration statements. The trial court had rejected an asserted assignment by TNA and had not reached the bank’s assignment; neither assignment issue was raised on appeal. The Alaska Supreme Court thus considered Avi-Truck’s own insurance rights without deciding assignments or every remaining dispute in the litigation.

sections.title: The Supreme Court implies rights for the contemplated owner
paragraphs: Justice Compton wrote for the Alaska Supreme Court. The insurers argued that an intended beneficiary required both parties’ intent at formation, yet Avi-Truck was then nonexistent and remained unknown to them until after the crash. The court agreed that nobody could specifically have intended that corporation when negotiations began. It did not invent an express agreement naming it.

Instead, insurance beneficiary rights could be implied at law when a third party belonged to the contemplated beneficiary class and recognizing it did not change the insured risk. Prior implied-co-insured cases made risk important, while decisions elsewhere allowed unnamed owners to recover where insurance protected ownership interests. The court preferred implication at law to reformation, which ordinarily corrected a mutual mistake to reflect clear intent. Absence of added risk alone was insufficient; class membership also mattered.

Both elements were present. TNA’s initial ownership plans were unsettled, and it sought coverage for itself or the eventual purchaser. By January 24 it owed Avi-Truck a contractual insurance duty. The same mechanics would maintain the plane and TNA would operate it whichever entity owned it, making Avi-Truck’s lack of its own carrier certificate irrelevant. Insurers contemplated protecting the ownership interest under those same operations. Avi-Truck therefore could sue directly.

sections.title: The pre-loss binder defeats the later airworthiness exclusion
paragraphs: The later policy excluded flight without an effective airworthiness certificate. The Supreme Court rejected the trial court’s view that this was ambiguous or merely required preserving whatever certification status existed at inception. It unambiguously required an existing, effective certificate; favoring coverage could not justify an unreasonable reading.

But the binder, not that later endorsement, was the written coverage document when the plane crashed. Insurers had agreed to cover cargo carriage by this particular aircraft. Competent inquiry would have revealed its certification limits, and its unusual features should have prompted investigation. There was no evidence of intentional misrepresentation; failing to volunteer information insurers never requested did not establish it. Chapman had made some inquiry and sent the risk to London without relaying his information because he expected further inquiry there.

Binders ordinarily incorporated usual policy terms, but TNA’s ordinary fleet policy was not usual for a plane practically unable to obtain the certificate for the contemplated use. The binder reasonably promised coverage for lawful government cargo carriage without that certificate. A post-loss exclusion destroying that coverage changed the bargain. The court reserved whether failure to investigate alone would defeat the exclusion had the policy been issued before the crash.

sections.title: The approved pilots and agency assurances support coverage
paragraphs: Insurers also invoked a pilot-certificate exclusion: the pilot lacked a large-aircraft type rating and the copilot lacked specified takeoffs and landings. Avi-Truck disputed whether federal rules imposed those requirements on public aircraft. The trial court thought they did but found a reasonable expectation of coverage. The Supreme Court affirmed on expectations and left federal applicability undecided.

Sudder’s operating and insurance experience did not make him an insurance expert; he relied on agents and understood coverage as a layperson. TNA employees had received Federal Aviation Administration assurances, including from legal counsel, that type ratings were unnecessary or unavailable for public aircraft. The binder specified hours and approval requirements without mentioning type ratings, and insurers discussed and approved the particular pilots’ credentials. Together these circumstances made the expectation of coverage objectively reasonable.

Testimony about the agency assurances was admitted to show the employees’ beliefs and conduct, not to prove the federal rules’ content. Because the relevant fact was that the statements were made and relied on, they were not hearsay for that purpose. The court did not declare the assurances legally correct. On March 30, 1984 it affirmed the $60,000 insurance judgment, with no separate writings.
